newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch on course for partial road pricing by 2001.
newsitem.headline: Dutch on course for partial road pricing by 2001.

text.p: Dutch Transport Minister Annemarie Jorritsma told a transport conference she advocated road pricing as a way of improving traffic flows and said the Netherlands was on course for partial road pricing by 2001.

"In 2000/2001 the Dutch government will, and I stress will, introduce road pricing on parts of the network. Other countries are setting up similar systems," she told the European Market for Infrastructural Projects conference on Tuesday.
Jorritsma said she was not in favour of large-scale construction of new roads as this was not a realistic option for such a small and densely populated country as the Netherlands.
Targeted construction aimed at opening up bottlenecks and filling in missing links would help eliminate traffic congestion in and around the major Dutch urban areas, she said.

Jorritsma said investment was being made to increase the efficiency of infrastructure use, including the designation of special peak period road lanes, speed limits linked to time periods and situation-specific traffic information boards.
Fixed costs paid by vehicle owners should be reduced and variable costs increased to tackle congestion, the minister told delegates. "The principle is 'he who drives pays'," she said.

Jorritsma told the conference the anticipated growth in traffic volumes which would accompany economic growth in the coming years would place a greater demand than ever on transport infrastructure in the Netherlands.
The Netherlands was faced with the problem of having to absorb the growth in traffic in a sustainable way, while at the same time giving priority to port and urban centre access.

"In practice this means we will have to invest more in infrastructure with the view to achieving more efficient use of existing transport networks," she said, adding this particularly applied to the use of roads for short-distance goods transport.

Individuals needed to be able to make a conscious choice of whether or not they used the private car. "To enable them to make such a choice, we need to invest in better, more efficient public transport," Jorritsma said.
Government had a clear role to play in making more efficient use of transport infrastructure, which also meant using more than one mode of transport in long distance goods transport.

"Most of the funding for these investments will have to come from national budgets. And given the financial condition of most European governments, this will mean looking at and re-adjusting public spending priorities," Jorritsma said. -- Keiron Henderson, Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000
